subject: spanish
title: At the café
scene: You arrive at a café in Oaxaca and want to order a coffee politely.
ask: Which sentence is natural?
why: Quisiera is an imperfect subjunctive form of querer used here as a polite request. The conditional querría is a different form. “Quiero un café” is also grammatical; quisiera softens the request.
hint: Choose a conjugated form of querer, not an English-style infinitive.
errors: “Estoy querer” combines estar with an unconjugated infinitive incorrectly.
Soy means I am (identity); it cannot order a coffee.
Tengo beber is missing que and expresses obligation, not a request.
transfer: Ask for the bill using “la cuenta”, then add “por favor”.

subject: spanish
title: The past in a sentence
scene: You are telling a friend about a finished trip yesterday.
ask: Complete: “Ayer ___ al mercado y ___ mangos.”
why: Fui and compré use the preterite for two completed events. Imperfect forms would set up habitual or ongoing background.
hint: Both verbs describe finished actions with a clear yesterday.
errors: The imperfect can describe background or habits but does not usually advance a sequence of completed events here.
Those are present tense forms.
Ser and tener do not mean go and buy.
transfer: Describe what you bought last week using compré and one food.

subject: spanish
title: Background versus interruption
scene: You were cooking when your friend called.
ask: Which sentence expresses the event naturally?
options: Estaba cocinó cuando mi amigo llamó.
why: Cocinaba frames cooking as an ongoing action; llamó is the completed interruption. “Estaba cocinando cuando llamó” also works.
hint: The ongoing action takes imperfect; the interruption takes preterite.
errors: This reverses the usual background/completed-event distinction.
Cocino means I cook in the present, so the tenses clash.
After estaba, use the gerund cocinando, not the preterite cocinó.
transfer: Translate “I was studying when it started raining.”

subject: spanish
title: Ser versus estar
scene: You are describing where your friend is today, not what they are like.
ask: Say “My friend is at home.”
why: Use estar for location: está en casa. Ser is used for identity, characteristics and typically the location of events, not a person’s ordinary location.
hint: We need a location, not an identity.
errors: Ser does not mark the ordinary location of a person.
Tener means to have.
Fue means went/was (past), not is (present).
transfer: Say “The concert is at the park” and explain why an event can use ser.

subject: spanish
title: A future plan
scene: Your teammate proposes dinner after you finish work.
ask: Choose the most direct way to say “We are going to eat after working.”
options: Vamos a comer después de trabajar.
why: Ir a + infinitive expresses a near-future plan: vamos a comer. Después de + infinitive means after doing something.
hint: Two patterns: ir + a + infinitive, después + de + infinitive.
errors: Both required prepositions are missing.
A finite past form comimos cannot follow iremos a.
Estar cannot be followed directly by infinitive to mean progressive.
transfer: Tell someone what you are going to do tomorrow using voy a + infinitive.

subject: spanish
title: The subjunctive in a wish
scene: You want a friend to arrive early; this is your wish, not a reported fact.
ask: Complete: “Espero que tú ___ temprano.”
why: Espero que introduces a desired but uncertain action, often triggering the present subjunctive llegues.
hint: A wish + que + a new subject calls for the subjunctive.
errors: Llegas is indicative and presents a factual/habitual arrival.
Llegaste is preterite, a completed past event.
Llegando is a gerund and cannot be the finite verb after tú.
transfer: Try “I hope they have time” using espero que tengan tiempo.

subject: piano
title: Find C on the keyboard
scene: Look at a group of two black keys on a piano.
ask: Where is C relative to that pair?
options: Immediately right of both black keys.
Immediately left of the first black key.
Two white keys to the right of the pair.
why: C sits just to the left of a two-black-key group. This pattern repeats across octaves.
hint: Find two black keys; the white note immediately before them is C.
errors: The white key after the pair is E.
The white key between them is D.
That points past D and E depending how you count.
transfer: Find every C across a real keyboard by looking for the two-black-key pattern.

subject: piano
title: Count one bar
scene: A 4/4 measure has four quarter-note beats.
ask: Which fills one complete measure?
options: One half note and one quarter note.
One dotted half note and one half note.
why: Each quarter note is one beat in 4/4; four equal four beats.
hint: Add the total number of beats; quarter=1, half=2, whole=4.
errors: 2+1=3 beats, leaving one beat.
Each whole note is four beats: total eight.
3+2=5 beats, too many.
transfer: Clap: ONE-and-TWO-and-THREE-and-FOUR-and at a steady tempo.

subject: piano
title: Build a major chord
scene: In C major, a tonic triad stacks the root, major third, and perfect fifth.
ask: Which notes make the C major chord?
why: C to E is four semitones; E to G is three. Those form a major triad.
hint: Start on C, skip D to E, then skip F to G.
errors: C–E♭–G makes C minor.
C–F–G is not a standard stacked-third triad.
C–E–A forms an A minor inversion rather than C major.
transfer: Build G major by stacking G–B–D. Play both chords if a keyboard is available.

subject: piano
title: Hear rhythm in numbers
scene: At 120 beats per minute, the metronome clicks twice per second.
ask: How many seconds does one quarter-note beat last?
why: 60 seconds / 120 beats = 0.5 seconds per beat. Tempo determines the duration of each beat.
hint: Divide 60 seconds by the beats per minute.

errors.2: Two is beats per second, not seconds per beat.
errors.120: You supplied beats per minute, not seconds.

transfer: Try at 80 BPM: a beat lasts 60/80=0.75 seconds.

subject: piano
title: Create tension and release
scene: In C major, a G7 chord tends to resolve to C.
ask: Which progression most clearly produces a dominant-to-tonic resolution?
why: G7 is V7 in C major. Its B and F tones create tension that commonly resolves into the C major tonic.
hint: Find V7 followed by I.
errors: C to Am shares notes but is not V7–I.
F to Dm is IV–ii.
C to F is I–IV, a departure rather than the expected return.
transfer: Play G–B–D–F followed by C–E–G and listen for the release.

subject: piano
title: Read intervals, not individual keys
scene: A melody moves C4 → E4 → G4 → E4 → C4.
ask: What structure makes this easy to remember?
options: Every step moves by one semitone.
An arpeggio of a C major triad.
why: C, E, G are the chord tones of C major. The melody climbs and descends an arpeggio instead of stepping through every scale note.
hint: Do these notes form a familiar chord?
errors: C→E moves four semitones; E→G moves three.
The pitches go up then down and skip notes.
The pattern is harmonically coherent and structured.
transfer: Try the same pattern on G–B–D–B–G.

subject: chess
title: Check the opponent’s threat
scene: Your opponent has a queen attacking an undefended rook. You can win a pawn with your bishop or save your rook.
ask: What should you examine first?
options: Check whether the rook is hanging and can be saved.
Move a random pawn to gain space.
why: Before pursuing your own plan, identify forcing threats, checks, captures, and undefended pieces. Losing a rook for a pawn is typically disastrous.
hint: Ask: what changed after the last move?
errors: A pawn is normally worth about 1 point and a rook 5; this ignores the immediate threat.
There is no reason to offer a draw in this position.
A space-gaining move does not address the rook.
transfer: Before every move scan checks, captures and attacks for both players.

subject: chess
title: Mate versus check
scene: A king is in check and has no legal king move, but the checking bishop can be captured by its own bishop.
ask: Is this checkmate?
options: Yes, because the king has no squares.
No, because capturing the attacker may end the check.
Yes, because a bishop is protected.
No, because kings cannot be checked.
why: Checkmate means no legal way to escape check: move the king, capture the attacker, or block the attack when possible.
hint: Can any legal move eliminate the check?
errors: The king need not move personally if another defender stops the check.
Nothing says the checking bishop is protected.
Kings can be checked but cannot be left in check.
transfer: When analyzing mate, list all checks, captures of attackers, and interpositions.

subject: chess
title: A fork wins material
scene: A knight moves with check and simultaneously attacks an opposing queen. The checked king must respond.
ask: What is the tactical idea?
why: A fork attacks two targets at once. Delivering check forces the king to respond and can leave the queen vulnerable next move.
hint: The knight attacks two important pieces with one move.
errors: A discovered attack happens when a moving piece unveils a line-piece attack.
A pin immobilizes or constrains a piece to protect something behind it.
Stalemate requires a side not in check to have no legal moves.
transfer: In every position look for knight checks that also hit heavy pieces.

subject: chess
title: The pinned defender
scene: A knight stands between its king and the opponent’s rook on the same open file.
ask: Why might that knight be unable to move?
options: Because moving would expose its own king to check.
Because a knight always defends its king.
why: This is an absolute pin: moving the knight would expose its king to the rook, an illegal move.
hint: Ask what the rook would attack if the knight disappeared.
errors: Knights can move in any L-shaped direction.
Rooks move along files and ranks, not diagonals.
There is no such general rule.
transfer: Find all line pieces aligned with a king and ask what intervenes.

subject: chess
title: Pawn opposition
scene: In a king-and-pawn ending, both kings face one another with one square between them, and it is your opponent’s turn to move.
ask: What is the key positional idea?
options: You have the opposition; the opponent may have to step aside.
The side with more space always loses.
Kings can stand next to each other.
why: The side NOT to move in this simple opposition arrangement generally has the opposition: the opponent must yield a square. This depends on the exact pawn structure.
hint: Who is forced to move first?
errors: Without other pieces, perpetual checks are generally unavailable.
Space alone does not decide the ending.
Kings may not be adjacent.
transfer: Set up two kings and a pawn and test whose turn changes the result.

subject: chess
title: Choose a candidate move
scene: You see a possible sacrifice with check, but cannot calculate a win. A safe development move is also available.
ask: Which process is strongest?
options: Sacrifice instantly: all checks are winning.
Calculate forcing replies and compare outcomes with the safe move.
Play the move that looks most aggressive.
why: Strong play compares candidate moves by calculating checks, captures, threats, and opponent responses, then evaluates resulting positions.
hint: Forcing moves deserve attention but still need verification.
errors: A check may be a blunder if the opponent has a strong reply.
Visual aggression is not a calculation.
Some sacrifices are objectively strong or necessary.
transfer: Pick two candidate moves and calculate at least two replies to each.

subject: calculus
title: Differentiate a polynomial
scene: You model daily output as f(x)=x³−4x²+2x.
ask: What is f′(2)?
hint: Use d/dx x^n = n x^(n−1) on each term.

errors.12: You only differentiated x³; include both remaining terms.
errors.-4: You omitted the derivative of 2x, which is +2.

transfer: Explain the units of a derivative: output units per unit of x.

subject: calculus
title: Instantaneous speed
scene: A bike’s position is s(t)=2t²+3t metres.
ask: Speed (velocity) in m/s at t=4?
hint: Differentiate position, then substitute t=4.

errors.44: That is position s(4), not instantaneous velocity.

transfer: How far did it move between t=3 and t=4? Compute s(4)−s(3).

subject: calculus
title: The chain rule
scene: A changing input is raised to a power.
ask: For f(x)=(2x+1)³, compute f′(2).
hint: Differentiate the outside, then multiply by derivative of the inside.

errors.75: You forgot to multiply by the inside derivative 2.
errors.30: You may have left the inner squared term uncomputed.

transfer: Explain why the chain rule needs the ×2 factor.

subject: calculus
title: Area under a rate
scene: Water enters a tank at r(t)=2t liters/min, from t=0 to t=3.
ask: How many liters arrive?
why: Integral_0^3 2t dt = [t²]_0^3 = 9 liters. The rising flow rate makes the area a triangle of base 3 and height 6.
hint: Integrate the rate or calculate triangle area under the rate graph.

errors.6: That is the rate at t=3 (L/min), not accumulated liters.
errors.18: You may have used a rectangle at the final flow rate.

transfer: Check with average flow rate (0+6)/2=3 L/min for 3 minutes.

subject: calculus
title: Optimize a product
scene: Profit before fixed costs is P(q)=40q−q² dollars, where q is a continuous quantity.
ask: At what q is P maximized?
why: P′(q)=40−2q=0, so q=20. P″=−2 < 0 confirms a maximum.
hint: At an interior optimum, marginal profit is zero.

errors.40: That ignores the derivative of the quadratic loss term.
errors.10: You may have dropped the factor 2 in d(q²)/dq.

transfer: Calculate the maximum profit P(20)=400 and compare P(19), P(21).

subject: calculus
title: Derivative of logarithm
scene: A logarithm wraps a quadratic expression.
ask: For f(x)=ln(x²+1), compute f′(1).
why: Chain rule: f′(x)=2x/(x²+1). Substituting 1 yields 2/2=1.
hint: For ln u, derivative is u′/u.

errors.2: You differentiated the inside but did not divide by the inside.
errors.0.5: You divided by 2 but lost the numerator 2x.

transfer: Derive d/dx ln(3x+2) with the same template.

subject: physics
title: Net force, not every force
scene: A 4 kg sled is pushed right with 22 N while friction pulls left with 6 N.
ask: Acceleration to the right?
why: Net force =22−6=16 N. Divide by 4 kg to get 4 m/s².
hint: Add signed forces before using F_net=ma.

errors.5.5: You used the push force and ignored friction.
errors.7: You added forces acting in opposite directions.

transfer: Double the mass while holding both forces: acceleration halves.

subject: physics
title: Velocity changes
scene: An object begins at 3 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 4 seconds.
ask: Final velocity?
hint: Start with initial velocity, then add acceleration times time.

errors.8: That is the change in velocity, not the final velocity.
errors.5: You forgot to multiply by time.

transfer: Find distance traveled: s=ut+½at².

subject: physics
title: Energy at the bottom
scene: A frictionless 2 kg object drops 5 m. Take g=10 m/s².
ask: How many joules of gravitational potential energy become kinetic?
why: Lost potential energy mgh=2·10·5=100 J becomes kinetic if other losses are absent.
hint: Use mgh; energy is in joules.

errors.50: You left out the 2 kg mass.
errors.10: You calculated g·h but forgot mass.

transfer: Explain why final speed does not depend on mass for this ideal drop.

subject: physics
title: Resistance in a circuit
scene: A 9 V battery is across a 3 Ω resistor.
ask: Current flowing through the resistor?
why: Ohm’s law I=V/R=9/3=3 amps.
hint: Voltage divided by resistance.

errors.27: That is V×R, the wrong operation.
errors.6: Subtracting resistance from voltage mixes unlike units.

transfer: If resistance doubles to 6 Ω, current falls to 1.5 A.

subject: physics
title: Conserve momentum
scene: A 2 kg cart moving right at 4 m/s collides and sticks to a 2 kg cart initially at rest.
ask: Shared final speed to the right?
why: Momentum initially is 2×4=8 kg·m/s. Combined mass is 4 kg, so v=8/4=2 m/s. Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
hint: Conserve momentum, then divide by combined mass.

errors.4: You ignored that both carts now move together.
errors.1: You divided by more total mass than exists.

transfer: Compute kinetic energy before and after to see the loss.

subject: physics
title: Circular motion requires force
scene: A 1 kg object travels in a horizontal circle at 6 m/s, radius 3 m.
ask: Magnitude of centripetal force?
why: F=m v²/r=1×36/3=12 N, directed toward the center.
hint: Square the speed before dividing by radius.

errors.2: You used v/r instead of v²/r.

transfer: Double the speed: centripetal force becomes four times as large.

subject: medicine
title: Triage comes before detail
scene: A patient arrives with shortness of breath, bluish lips, and altered mental status.
ask: Which is the safest first action?
options: Ask for a detailed diet history.
Urgently assess airway, breathing, circulation and call for emergency help.
Delay evaluation until the next appointment.
why: This is a time-critical presentation. In real life activate emergency medical services and assess ABCs; do not wait for a detailed history.
hint: Treat immediate threats to life before fine diagnostic distinctions.
errors: A diet history is not the first priority during possible respiratory failure.
Delaying could be dangerous.
A lipid panel is not time-critical in this presentation.
transfer: Practice identifying which symptoms change the urgency of a case.

subject: medicine
title: Differentiate signs and diagnoses
scene: An adult reports fatigue. One isolated laboratory result is mildly abnormal.
ask: What is the best general principle?
options: The abnormal value proves a diagnosis.
Interpret the finding alongside symptoms, examination, context and repeated or corroborating tests.
Every abnormal result is an emergency.
Ignore all tests and use symptoms alone.
why: Tests modify clinical probability; context, pretest probability and measurement variability matter. A single result often does not establish a diagnosis.
hint: Consider the whole picture and the possibility of measurement variation.
errors: A single abnormality often has several potential explanations.
Severity depends on which value, how abnormal it is and symptoms.
Tests can provide essential evidence when interpreted appropriately.
transfer: Ask what else you would need to know before interpreting an abnormal result.

subject: medicine
title: Sensitivity and false negatives
scene: A test with 90% sensitivity is used on 100 people who truly have a disease.
ask: On average, how many false negatives?
why: Sensitivity is P(test positive | disease). Out of 100 affected people, 90 test positive and 10 test negative.
hint: False negative fraction = 1−sensitivity.

errors.90: That is the expected true-positive count.

transfer: Explain why sensitivity by itself cannot tell you the chance a positive is truly diseased.

subject: medicine
title: Bayes in clinical decisions
scene: A very rare disease has a screening test that is usually accurate. A positive result appears in someone with low prior risk.
ask: What must you consider before calling it a definitive diagnosis?
options: Prevalence (prior probability) and the false-positive rate.
Whether the patient prefers the result to be positive.
why: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence, sensitivity, and specificity. For rare conditions, false positives may comprise a large share of positives.
hint: A test result changes a starting probability—it does not create certainty.
errors: Sensitivity alone ignores false positives.
Cost matters to decisions but does not establish diagnostic certainty.
Wishes do not establish test validity.
transfer: Draw a 1,000-person frequency table to see false positives concretely.

subject: medicine
title: Clinical differential diagnosis
scene: Chest pain can reflect cardiac, respiratory, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal or other causes.
ask: What is a sound initial reasoning approach?
options: Choose the most familiar benign cause.
Rapidly assess dangerous possibilities and red flags, then narrow with history, examination and appropriate tests.
Use one symptom to diagnose with certainty.
Defer attention to red flags until the final exam.
why: Clinical reasoning combines risk prioritization and probability. Potentially life-threatening etiologies must be considered promptly even if common benign causes exist.
hint: Safety and prevalence both matter, in that order when urgency is high.
errors: Familiarity is a cognitive bias, not a diagnostic method.
Many conditions share symptoms.
Red flags affect immediate triage.
transfer: List three questions that would distinguish urgent from nonurgent presentations.

subject: medicine
title: Evidence strength
scene: A treatment looks impressive in ten uncontrolled anecdotes, while a larger randomized controlled trial shows no clear benefit.
ask: Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: The controlled evidence deserves greater weight, while checking trial quality, effect sizes and applicability.
No study can provide useful evidence.
why: Without controls, regression to the mean, placebo effects and selection bias can create misleading apparent benefit. Randomization is not perfect but better addresses confounding.
hint: Ask which evidence best separates treatment effect from what would happen anyway.
errors: Anecdotes lack control of confounding and chance.
Absence of clear benefit does not by itself imply harm.
Evidence quality differs across studies.
transfer: Explain the difference between clinical significance and statistical significance.

subject: history
title: Primary source with a purpose
scene: A government report praises its own economic program during an election.
ask: What should a historian do first?
options: Treat its numbers and claims as automatically neutral.
Ask who produced it, for whom, why, and compare independent sources.
why: A source can contain valuable facts and motivated framing. Provenance, intended audience and corroboration let us use it critically without discarding it.
hint: Who has an interest in making this account persuasive?
errors: Official status does not remove incentive to persuade.
Biased sources can still reveal facts and the author’s intentions.
Skepticism does not justify making the opposite assumption.
transfer: Look for a contemporary opposing source and identify what both agree on.

subject: history
title: Chronology and cause
scene: An economic crash occurs just before a government falls.
ask: Does the sequence prove the crash caused the collapse?
options: Yes, anything earlier caused what followed.
No; test plausible mechanisms and competing explanations.
Only if both happened in the same year.
why: Post hoc does not imply causation. Investigate mechanisms, contemporaneous evidence and rival influences.
hint: Sequence is necessary for a cause but not sufficient.
errors: Temporal order alone cannot exclude confounders or coincidence.
Same-year timing does not identify causation.
Historical causal inference is possible, though uncertain.
transfer: Find one mechanism and one rival cause for this hypothetical collapse.

subject: history
title: Survivorship bias
scene: Most surviving written records about an empire come from wealthy literate elites.
ask: What is the greatest interpretive risk?
options: The empire had no ordinary people.
Treating elite perspectives as representative of everyone.
why: Preservation and literacy create a selective archive. Material culture, oral tradition and other sources can reveal neglected experiences.
hint: Whose experiences rarely made it into the archive?
errors: The archive is incomplete, not proof of absence.
Written evidence can still be informative.
Archaeology often helps correct textual silences.
transfer: Propose one nonwritten source for studying everyday life.

subject: history
title: Independent corroboration
scene: Three newspaper articles repeat the same eyewitness account almost word for word.
ask: How many independent eyewitness sources do you actually have?
options: Three, because there are three publications.
One, unless the accounts have independent origins.
why: Repeated publication does not multiply independent observations. Tracing claims back to their origin is crucial to avoid false confidence.
hint: Distinguish copies from independently obtained observations.
errors: Copies share the same underlying evidence.
One firsthand account may still be valuable.
Publication records and attribution can often reveal origins.
transfer: Draw a source genealogy: which articles cite which original report?

subject: history
title: Counterfactual discipline
scene: You propose that one reform caused an empire to survive a century longer.
ask: What makes this counterfactual more credible?
options: Describe a plausible mechanism and compare similar cases or constraints while acknowledging uncertainty.
Remove all other variables by imagining them away.
Avoid evidence because the alternative never happened.
why: Counterfactuals cannot be observed directly, but they can be constrained by known resources, institutions, mechanisms and comparative cases.
hint: Constrain the imagined world with what you know about the real one.
errors: Confidence does not substitute for evidence.
Other variables and unintended consequences must be considered.
Evidence about real-world mechanisms still matters.
transfer: List two constraints that might prevent the reform from working.

subject: history
title: Numbers without context
scene: A city’s recorded crime count doubles after authorities redefine several minor offenses as crimes.
ask: What is the responsible interpretation?
options: The change in definitions may explain some or all of the increase; seek comparable measures.
The report is worthless in every respect.
why: Measurement practices and category boundaries can create structural breaks. Historians compare consistent definitions and alternative sources before drawing conclusions.
hint: Has the thing being counted stayed the same?
errors: The statistical series may not be comparable across the change.
What qualifies for a category determines counts.
The report can still be informative with proper qualification.
transfer: Identify a second source that could check the trend.

subject: economics
title: Opportunity cost in dollars
scene: A freelance project pays $600. Accepting it means turning down your next best project paying $450, with equal effort and costs.
ask: What is the incremental monetary benefit of choosing the $600 project?
why: The relevant comparison is the best forgone alternative. $600−$450=$150, not $600.
hint: Compare with the next best option, not with doing nothing.

errors.600: That is gross revenue, not incremental benefit over the alternative.
errors.450: That is the value forgone, not the gain.

transfer: Ask what nonmonetary benefits or risks might reverse your choice.

subject: economics
title: Price and demand
scene: The price of a product rises, while tastes and incomes stay the same.
ask: In the basic demand model, what changes?
options: Quantity demanded typically falls along the same demand curve.
why: The law of demand describes movement along a demand curve when the product’s own price changes, all else equal.
hint: Price change: move along a curve, not shift it.
errors: A demand-curve shift requires a change in another determinant.
Supply response depends on producers and market conditions.
An upward-sloping demand response is not the standard case.
transfer: Name one factor that shifts demand without changing the product’s price.

subject: economics
title: Real versus nominal return
scene: A savings account earns 6% nominal over a year and inflation is 3%. Approximate real return using the Fisher approximation.
ask: Approximate real return in percent?
why: Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation = 6−3=3%. Exact is 1.06/1.03−1≈2.91%.
hint: Subtract inflation from nominal growth for an approximation.

errors.6: That is nominal return before inflation.
errors.9: You added inflation rather than removing purchasing-power erosion.

transfer: Calculate the exact return using (1.06/1.03)−1.

subject: economics
title: Elasticity intuition
scene: A seller raises price 10% and units sold fall 20%, with other factors roughly constant.
ask: What does that suggest about own-price elasticity magnitude?
why: Elasticity ≈ %ΔQ / %ΔP = −20/10=−2; the magnitude 2 exceeds 1 (elastic).
hint: Compare percent quantity change to percent price change.
errors: Quantity responded proportionally more than price changed.
Zero elasticity means no quantity response.
Sales can fall with a price rise.
transfer: Estimate what happens to revenue when demand is elastic and price rises.

subject: economics
title: Comparative advantage
scene: Worker A can make 8 shirts or 4 bags per day. Worker B can make 6 shirts or 6 bags.
ask: How many shirts does A give up to make one bag?
why: A trades 8 shirts for 4 bags, so opportunity cost is 8/4=2 shirts per bag. B gives up 1 shirt per bag; B has comparative advantage in bags.
hint: Divide shirts foregone by bags gained.

errors.0.5: That is bags per shirt, the reciprocal.
errors.1: That is B’s opportunity cost, not A’s.

transfer: Determine who has comparative advantage in shirts.

subject: economics
title: Trade-offs and externalities
scene: A factory can produce cheaply but imposes pollution costs on neighbors that buyers and sellers do not pay.
ask: What is this called?
options: An opportunity cost only to the factory.
why: A negative externality is an unpriced cost imposed on third parties. Market prices can understate total social cost.
hint: Who bears the cost outside the transaction?
errors: A network effect concerns the value to users from other users.
With unpriced external costs, private equilibrium can be socially inefficient.
The factory and buyers may not pay neighbors’ costs.
transfer: Compare a pollution tax with a direct emissions standard.

subject: business
title: Profit per box
scene: A 12-pack sells for $18. Ingredients and co-packing cost $7, fulfillment $3, and payment fees $1 per box. Exclude fixed overhead.
ask: Contribution margin per box?
why: Contribution = $18−$7−$3−$1=$7 before fixed costs, customer acquisition and taxes.
hint: Subtract every variable cost from selling price.

errors.11: You subtracted production cost but missed shipping and payment fees.
errors.8: You missed one of the $1 transaction costs.

transfer: What happens if you run a $3 discount without changing costs?

subject: business
title: A margin is a ratio
scene: A product sells for $20 and has $12 total variable cost.
ask: Contribution margin percentage?
why: Contribution dollars = $8. Margin rate = $8/$20=0.40 or 40%.
hint: Use profit per unit divided by revenue per unit.

errors.8: That is margin dollars, not the percentage.
errors.60: That is variable cost as a percent of price.

transfer: Compare gross margin with contribution margin: which variable costs are included?

subject: business
title: Break-even acquisition
scene: Your first-order contribution margin is $14, and the customer typically places no repeat orders. Ignore other customer-level costs.
ask: Maximum break-even customer acquisition cost (CAC)?
why: At CAC=$14, first-order contribution after acquisition is zero. Spending more loses money on the customer under these assumptions.
hint: Do not confuse selling price with contribution after variable costs.

errors.30: Revenue is not the amount available to pay for acquisition.
errors.0: Positive contribution can cover some CAC.

transfer: How does an expected second purchase change the ceiling after accounting for retention?

subject: business
title: Conversion as a funnel
scene: 1,000 qualified visitors see a product page. 4% buy, with one order each.
ask: How many orders?
why: Conversion=40/1,000=4%. Multiply traffic by conversion rate: 1,000×0.04=40.
hint: Convert 4% to 0.04 before multiplying.
transfer: Estimate the order change if conversion rises from 4% to 5%.

subject: business
title: Retention and unit economics
scene: A customer’s first order contributes $8. Half of customers make exactly one repeat purchase with $10 contribution. No more orders; ignore discounting.
ask: Expected lifetime contribution before acquisition?
why: Expected contribution = $8+0.5×$10=$13. Use a probability-weighted future contribution, not a guaranteed reorder.
hint: First contribution + retention probability × repeat contribution.

errors.10: That omits the guaranteed first order.

transfer: If CAC is $11, expected contribution after acquisition is $2.

subject: business
title: The moat question
scene: A branded food product gets one-time influencer attention but weak repeat purchases.
ask: Which evidence would most directly improve the long-term business case?
options: A viral post with no attributable sales.
Cohort repeat purchase rates and contribution after fulfillment and acquisition.
Higher gross sales without looking at costs.
why: Durable products need demonstrable repeat demand and healthy contribution economics. Attention can fuel trial, but retention and unit economics determine repeatable value.
hint: Distinguish one-time trial from profitable habit.
errors: Reach without sales attribution does not establish product-market fit.
Packaging might help conversion but does not prove ongoing demand.
Top-line revenue without costs can hide losses.
transfer: Specify a simple 30/60/90-day repeat purchase cohort report.

subject: life
title: A useful experiment
scene: You are considering a new hobby but do not know if you enjoy it.
ask: Which decision creates information at low cost?
options: Buy a year of lessons before ever trying.
Try one 20-minute beginner session and notice what was enjoyable and confusing.
Decide you will either become elite or never start.
Wait until every possible resource is perfect.
why: A small reversible trial reduces uncertainty and provides real behavioral evidence without major commitment.
hint: Favor a small reversible test when uncertainty is high.
errors: Large irreversible commitment occurs before learning what fits.
All-or-nothing thinking can block discovery.
Perfect preparation cannot substitute for experience.
transfer: Define one small experiment you can run tomorrow.

subject: life
title: Separating outcome and process
scene: You made a thoughtful decision with the information available; it turned out poorly due to a rare event.
ask: What should you conclude?
options: The decision process was necessarily bad.
Evaluate the reasoning and probabilities separately from the single outcome.
why: A decision can be rational ex ante yet fail ex post. Judge calibration and method over repeated decisions, not a single lucky or unlucky outcome.
hint: Was the risk understood before the outcome?
errors: A bad outcome does not logically prove bad reasoning.
Random events affect individual results.
Risk avoidance is not the same as good judgment.
transfer: Record a forecast before an important decision and review it later.

subject: life
title: Expected value as a guide
scene: A reversible project has a 30% chance of earning $1,000 and a 70% chance of losing $100. Ignore nonmonetary factors.
ask: Expected monetary value?
why: EV=0.3×1,000+0.7×(−100)=300−70=230 dollars. Positive EV is not a guarantee.
hint: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add.

errors.900: You subtracted a raw loss without weighting probabilities.

transfer: Discuss why a positive EV project can still be inappropriate if losses are unaffordable.

subject: life
title: Causal habit design
scene: You keep forgetting to practice piano after work.
ask: Which change most directly reduces the behavioral friction?
options: Leave the keyboard accessible and tie a five-minute practice to a reliable daily cue.
Set an immediate three-hour daily target.
why: A stable cue and reduced setup friction make the desired action easier to start. Tiny successful repetitions support skill acquisition more than an unsustainable plan.
hint: Make the first five minutes easy and automatic.
errors: Self-criticism often increases avoidance.
Huge initial targets can make practice feel costly.
Tools are useful only if they change the actual behavior.
transfer: Pick one existing daily cue and name the smallest practice action.

subject: life
title: Avoid false precision
scene: Two life plans differ in happiness, income stability, relationships, and time. You cannot measure all of these precisely.
ask: What is the most useful comparison?
options: Give every value an arbitrary dollar price and claim certainty.
State assumptions, identify nonnegotiables, stress-test different scenarios, and try reversible parts first.
Choose only the higher expected income.
Refuse to decide until prediction is perfect.
why: Multi-criteria decisions can be approached with explicit trade-offs and scenario analysis without pretending all values reduce to one precise number.
hint: Which considerations could change the decision under another scenario?
errors: Precise-looking numbers can hide fragile assumptions.
Income alone may not capture the objective.
Some uncertainty cannot be eliminated before deciding.
transfer: Write down one assumption that would make you change your mind.

subject: life
title: Review a learning plateau
scene: You have practiced for a month but progress has slowed.
ask: Which adjustment is most likely to produce useful learning?
options: Identify the exact failure pattern, isolate it in short deliberate drills, then retest in varied contexts.
Switch subjects every time something is hard.
Hide your mistakes from your teacher.
why: Expertise grows through feedback-rich deliberate practice near the edge of current ability, followed by transfer back to authentic work.
hint: Diagnose the failure, train it, test it again.
errors: Comfortable repetition can consolidate basics but rarely challenges weak points.
Avoidance prevents correction.
Without error information it is hard to target practice.
transfer: Describe one mistake you make repeatedly and design a five-minute corrective drill.

subject: books
title: Find the claim
scene: A paragraph reads: “The library should stay open later. Students who work day shifts often cannot visit during existing hours.”
ask: Which sentence gives the main claim?
options: The library should stay open later.
why: The first sentence states what the author wants us to accept. The second offers a reason. Distinguishing claim from support makes reading active.
hint: Which statement is the author trying to persuade you to accept?
errors: This is supporting evidence, not the proposed conclusion.
The text does not assert this as its argument.
Nothing in the paragraph supports that reading.
transfer: State the author’s claim in one sentence, then identify the supporting evidence.

subject: books
title: What is a counterargument?
scene: An essay argues that remote work improves productivity in some sectors.
ask: Which is a legitimate counterargument?
options: Some tasks depend on spontaneous in-person collaboration that is harder to replicate remotely.
The author must be wrong because they are optimistic.
why: A counterargument addresses the central claim by providing competing evidence, a limitation or alternative explanation.
hint: Challenge the causal claim rather than the author.
errors: This is unrelated to productivity.
Punctuation is irrelevant.
Attacking the author’s mood is not evidence.
transfer: Write a fair steelman of the essay before criticizing it.

subject: books
title: Distinguish inference from statement
scene: A narrator never says she fears the sea, but repeatedly avoids boats and changes the subject when asked about sailing.
ask: Which is the strongest supported reading?
options: It is certain she drowned in a previous life.
The text suggests unease about the sea, though the cause remains uncertain.
She secretly owns a boat business.
Her behavior proves the narrator is lying.
why: Close reading draws cautious inferences from repeated textual evidence. Avoid inventing backstory beyond what is supported.
hint: What is shown and what is merely plausible?
errors: The text gives no evidence for this backstory.
No textual support.
Avoidance does not establish a lie.
transfer: Point to two details supporting the cautious inference.

subject: books
title: Find a hidden assumption
scene: An op-ed says, “This bestseller sold a million copies; therefore it is the best-written novel of the decade.”
ask: Which assumption is doing the heavy lifting?
why: The conclusion treats popularity as a direct proxy for literary merit. That needs evidence; sales also reflect distribution, marketing and trends.
hint: What connects copies sold to quality?
errors: This fact does not bridge popularity and merit.
Paperback formats do not bridge popularity and merit.
This is irrelevant to the inference.
transfer: Decide what literary criteria would count as independent evidence.

subject: books
title: Interpret a metaphor
scene: An essay calls memory “a museum with changing exhibits.”
ask: What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: Memory stores perfectly fixed records forever.
What we recall is selected and reorganized over time.
The author rejects all historical facts.
why: The metaphor emphasizes curated, shifting selection. Good interpretation respects the words of the image without stretching beyond the text.
hint: What does a museum do with its exhibits?
errors: “Changing exhibits” specifically challenges fixity.
This is not implied by the metaphor.
A metaphor about memory does not reject factual inquiry.
transfer: Explain where the metaphor helps and where it might mislead.

subject: books
title: Compare arguments fairly
scene: Two authors disagree over a historical event. One cites official records; the other studies oral testimony.
ask: Which evaluation is strongest?
options: Compare provenance, purpose, representativeness and possible blind spots in both forms of evidence.
Choose the author whose prose you like more.
why: Different sources answer different questions and have different failure modes. Evidence evaluation requires attention to methods, incentives, and gaps.
hint: Ask what each source can and cannot tell you.
errors: Official records may be selective or motivated.
Memory and testimony can also be selective or mistaken.
Prose quality does not establish truth.
transfer: List a question each source type can answer particularly well.
